newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese drug firms brace for drug price cuts.
newsitem.headline: Japanese drug firms brace for drug price cuts.

text.p: Japan's drug makers and wholesalers are bracing for painful price cuts as the government tries to trim the huge cost of state medical funding.

In conjunction with an increase in Japan's sales tax next April, the government is planning to review the pricing system under which it reimburses hospitals for the drugs they dispense, and the result is likely to be a cut in the rates.

Analysts say the official drug prices set under the National Health Insurance (NHI) system will likely be reduced by an average of three percent next April, putting pressure on the profitability of big pharmaceuticals firms.
"It would be a considerable blow to both makers and wholesalers if the government plans to revise drug prices," said an official of Shionogi and Co Ltd, the fifth largest Japanese drug maker.
Under rules set in 1987, the NHI drug prices are usually revised every two years. Prices were last reviewed in April this year, when prices were cut by an average of 6.8 percent.

The next revision should not be due for another two years but the health ministry decided last month to revise its health payment rates, including drug prices and clinical charges, next April when the consumption tax rate is raised to five percent from the current three percent, ministry officials said.

A cut in the official drug prices hurts drug makers' earnings. As a result of the last revision, analysts say that several top-ranking firms such as Ono Pharmaceuticals Co Ltd and Chugai Pharmaceutical Co Ltd will likely see their current profits fall in the 1996/97 business year from the previous year's levels.
When the three percent sales tax was first introduced in Japan in 1989, the government actually increased NHI drug prices to avoid fanning controversy over the tax move.

But this time the government -- keen to rein in spending due to tight budgetary conditions -- is likely to take advantage of a gap between market prices and NHI prices to justify a cut in the official rates.

A spokesman for Suzuken Co Ltd, Japan's largest wholesaler of pharmaceuticals, noted last week that drugs are currently retailed to hospitals and other medical facilities at around 15-16 percent below the NHI rates.

"Assuming that the government...will allow an 11 percent difference between the official and market rates, the NHI drug prices will likely be lowered by around three percent," said Yasuhiro Nakazawa, analyst at Nikko Research Centre.

The government currently allows an 11 percent price gap because medical institutions rely heavily on the profit they make as a result of buying drugs at prices below the rate at which they are reimbursed by the government.

But the system has been criticised as providing an incentive for hospitals to prescribe excessive amounts of drugs. Japan's drug costs, which account for larger portion of overall medical spending than in other industrialised nations, are largely blamed for a rising state medical bill.

Analysts and pharmaceutical company officials said next April's extraordinary drug-price revision gives the government an opportunity to keep costs under control -- an ever more pressing task in a rapidly ageing society.

Masatake Miyoshi, analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc, said the impact of the price cut on drug makers and wholesalers depends on whether the government softens the blow by raising the reimbursement rates for clinical charges. "A hike in clinical charges would ease the pressure on wholesalers to give discounts on the drugs they supply to hospitals," said Miyoshi.
